name: Amira Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, political parties, AI firms or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side, and this conversation is confidential. What is a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a small policy amendments desk for an insurer. I have a bachelor's degree, but the useful skill is finding which clause changed between two versions of a policy. I use AI every day to compare drafts, then mark the source page before approving a letter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy and what tires you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like teaching a new clerk to find the clause instead of trusting my answer. Repeating a correction because nobody read the original policy wears me down. My pay is good, I have nine months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of insurers near our town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the tool where it helps and keep a clerk responsible for each amendment. A faster comparison gives us time to clear the old correction box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own lead role and income look safe over the next few years. Routine sorting might leave a junior vacancy empty, but my savings and nearby insurers mean I need not panic about a small change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd record where the comparison tool misses a clause and show two examples at Friday's desk meeting. In the first year of this mild change I'd keep my paid lead work and give new clerks practice on the original policy pages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I want tools that earn their place, not another screen merely because somebody sold it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show your manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our trainee Elise once caught a date the software skipped. I would put that correction beside the tool's summary so the manager sees why a person signs the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a better tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not spend my own reserve on an insurer's software. Nine months saved is for my own living costs if work changes, not for the company's budget.

say: I'd use the **comparison tool** where it earns its place.
I'd keep a **named clerk** responsible for each amendment.
think: My **lead income** looks safe in the near term.
I see a **junior vacancy** staying empty even with modest automation.
do: Record **missed clauses** and show two examples this Friday.
Keep **paid lead work** and train clerks on source pages.
feel: **Calm** about her own work and money.
S0.quote: A faster comparison gives us time to clear the old correction box.
fieldNote: She uses **AI daily** but checks the original policy before approval.
Her **nine-month reserve** and abundant local insurers support confidence.
She teaches **source reading** rather than making trainees rely on her answers.

steps.text: Show two missed policy clauses at Friday desk meeting
Continue paid lead amendments and train clerks on original pages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team writing and checking policy letters are exactly the tasks software will take first. A person should still be paid to verify an exclusion before a customer signs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose some hours if the insurer decides one lead can cover two desks. I have a cushion, but I cannot call a shorter paycheque harmless merely because I saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd compare a month of amendment errors before and after the tool and ask the manager what paid checking posts remain. In the first year after the change, if my hours fall, I'd apply to advertised paid policy review roles at nearby insurers after checking their pay and entry rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possible cut to my own hours. I would rather test a real vacancy than argue that my title deserves protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would learning the new system save you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI already, so another tutorial alone is not a career plan. I would learn a new approved system if the insurer requires it, but only after seeing how staff catch its mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your sister help with the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister might offer advice, but she cannot promise my rent. I would keep the current job until a written offer shows enough pay to cover my living costs.

I'd ask which **paid checking posts** remain after automation.
think: My **hours could fall** if two desks are combined.
My strong cushion helps me search, but **pay still matters**.
do: Compare **amendment errors** across one month now.
Apply for **advertised paid review roles** if hours fall after change.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic cut in her own hours.
S1.quote: I would rather test a real vacancy than argue that my title deserves protection.
fieldNote: She prefers **practical proof** of errors and paid vacancies.
She uses AI daily; learning an **employer-required system** is conditional, not a new habit.
She keeps **current wages** until a written offer covers living costs.

steps.text: Compare one month of policy amendment errors before and after tool use
Apply to advertised paid insurer roles meeting pay and entry rules if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches policy reasoning in our office before robots arrive around 2031. The robot date does not give a paperwork clerk three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose this lead post if the insurer trusts cheaper AGI with full amendments. Nine months of expenses and many local insurers give me room to search, but none of those firms owes me a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep my current wages, save the next three monthly transfers and ask the insurer for its staffing plan. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my post ends, I'd apply only for advertised paid review roles that accept my degree and cover my rent; I'd seek public support only if eligible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not without a route. A possible job loss is serious even when I have savings to bridge it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a business instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not launch a business on borrowed money because of a scenario card. I would first check what paid insurers actually need and whether my experience meets their entry rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you decide at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner to keep our current lease while my pay exists. My partner earns now, but I cannot budget future rent on a wage we have not agreed will continue.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches our policy work first.
I'd ask the insurer for a **written staffing plan**.
think: I **could lose my post**, but no decision has been made.
My nine months of savings buys time, not a **promised vacancy**.
do: Keep **current wages** and save three monthly transfers now.
Apply for **paid review vacancies** meeting entry and rent needs if cut.
Seek **eligible public support** during a post-loss search.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible loss of her own post.
S2.quote: Nine months of expenses and many local insurers give me room to search, but none of those firms owes me a vacancy.
fieldNote: She separates a **possible layoff** from a settled one.
She rejects a **borrowed business** and checks paid work first.
Partner income exists **now**, without a guarantee after 2028.

steps.text: Save the next three monthly transfers from current paid work
Apply for posted paid review jobs meeting degree and rent needs if cut
Seek public support only if eligible during a post-loss search

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives five years to see which insurer will still pay a person to check hard clauses. Robots around 2034 still do little to delay office work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My near-term salary looks secure, though I may need a different paid role by 2031. I have choices nearby and time to build skill, but I will not count an invented job as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the compliance manager what qualification and wage a posted policy audit role requires and keep training juniors on source clauses. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my desk closes, I'd apply to real paid audit openings only if I meet their entry rules and the pay covers my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own paid role by 2031, though the reserve and five years give me room to prepare. I can check real openings without changing our household plans on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for an audit course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may take a short audit course if a real paid post requires it and the fee fits my savings. I would not enrol just for a certificate; I would get the entry rules in writing first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your father help you financially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father ran his own shop and taught me to keep accounts before taking a risk. He could offer advice, but I would not assume he has wages for me or cash to replace my salary.

say: I'd check **paid audit roles** before buying a course.
I'd say **2034 robots** do not shelter policy desks.
think: My **near-term salary** is safe, though 2031 may require a move.
I value family advice, but cannot count it as a **future wage**.
do: Check **audit qualification and pay** against a posted role this year.
Apply for **real paid audit openings** if displaced after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about her own 2031 wages, with savings and time to act.
S3.quote: I will not count an invented job as income.
fieldNote: She checks **written entry rules** and wages before any course.
Her father offers **advice**, not assumed financial rescue.
The five-year window supports a **measured paid search**.

steps.text: Check qualification and wage for posted policy audit jobs this year
Apply for posted paid audit work meeting rent and entry rules if cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 is enough time to plan carefully, if the insurer gives us honest staffing figures. Robots in 2039 still arrive after office reasoning changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead salary and work look secure for the next few years. At 37 I would still need paid work; I might be in another insurer by then, but a decade is not a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the coming year I'd keep an annual record of amendment errors and ask for the firm's staffing forecast. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd stay in a paid review role if it exists; if it ends, I'd contact nearby insurers only about advertised roles meeting my pay and qualifications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, watchful about a decade away. My reserve lets me make decisions after seeing facts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should new clerks learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep teaching the new clerk to compare policies herself. A good apprenticeship at the desk is worth more than a glossy course with no employer behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend savings on training or a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could invest in training if a posted paid role requires it, but I would check the fee and the actual vacancy first. I would not turn my savings into a speculative software business.

say: I'd ask the insurer for **staffing figures** each year, rather than take a distant promise about the desk.
I'd keep **desk apprenticeships** for new clerks.
think: My **near-term lead pay** looks secure, although I cannot say the same for the whole decade.
At 37 I still need **paid work**, not a pension story.
do: Record **amendment errors** and request a staffing forecast this year.
Keep **paid review work** after 2036 if the role survives.
Contact **nearby insurers** if displaced, checking advertised pay and qualifications.
S4.quote: A good apprenticeship at the desk is worth more than a glossy course with no employer behind it.
fieldNote: She values **practical desk teaching** and paid work over unsupported credentials.
Her **near-term salary** remains secure despite 2036 uncertainty.
Any training spend is **conditional** on a real vacancy and affordable fee.

steps.text: Record amendment errors and ask insurer for staffing forecast this year
Continue paid policy review if her role exists after 2036
Contact nearby insurers about advertised paid roles if displaced after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the insurer could cut my post before I test another paid route. An honest staffing plan and real vacancies with pay and entry rules would help; eligible temporary support would cover a gap.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the amended letter when software compares the policies. Someone still needs to own an exclusion a customer can lose money over. I want that responsibility named, even if the desk changes.

headlineQuote: Someone still needs to own an exclusion a customer can lose money over.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old policy lead** with a bachelor's degree and a habit of checking source clauses.
She uses **AI daily**, earns high pay, has nine months saved and can approach many nearby insurers.
She values **desk apprenticeships** and measured personal initiative more than costly credentials without jobs.
Her own near-term income feels **secure**; possible shorter hours or job loss make faster change anxious.
She seeks **advertised paid work** subject to entry, rent and vacancy checks, while keeping current wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her lead post before she tests another paid route.
whatWouldHelp: An honest **staffing plan** and real paid vacancies with entry rules would help.
Eligible **temporary support** could bridge any job gap.
